title: Anthropic report shows how pushing AI at work can backfire
excerpt: An Anthropic report finds top-down AI rollouts can give managers more power to track performance — and spark employee pushback.
content_html:
Anthropic says leaders pushing AI can make workers feel watched

By Tim Paradis

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-24T18:00:52.819Z

When bosses push AI, they can fuel surveillance fears and cause resistance from workers, an Anthropic report found.

Researchers at the AI startup conducted 66 interviews with 58 companies that are Anthropic customers, and found that pushback can lead to "abandoned or fragile automations."

The quotes sprinkled throughout the 29-page report offered a snapshot of how the companies are adopting AI. It comes as some firms have cited AI in making job cuts, and as uncertainty about the technology's impact leaves many feeling stuck in a broader low-hire, low-fire labor market.

AI implementation isn't always seamless, as companies experiment with new processes. At one law firm, Anthropic said, the chief operating officer asked a staffer to create an AI tool to check for conflicts of interest. That left workers handling tricky cases they'd previously handed off to attorneys. Eventually, when workers pushed back, the firm ditched the tool and resumed the prior process, the report said.

Other managers used AI to keep closer tabs on workers. One operations supervisor told researchers he began each day with an AI-generated report on how much work each member of his 12-person team completed and how often they made errors. "If somehow there was a lag, then I can question back to them, 'Okay, what happened this hour?'" the leader told Anthropic.

Some interviewees thought AI could make performance feedback more accurate, yet also worried about how closely it could let bosses track employees.

Companies reported hiring less

People at two-thirds of the companies told Anthropic they were hiring less because of AI. "We may not be firing, but we're not hiring," one interviewee said.

A third of these decreases came from companies leaving roles unfilled after workers left, though most stemmed from companies skipping hires they would have made without AI, the report said.

That was in line with prior findings, Anthropic said, that "AI-native" startups employ fewer people. One engineering leader at a health management company said, "We've added a lot of capacity by buying tokens instead of hiring people."

Some companies went further. Interviewees at five companies also discussed pushing out workers who wouldn't adopt AI. At two companies, interviewees said AI automation eliminated a position, resulting in someone losing their job.

An engineering leader highlighted the differences he saw emerge between those who embraced AI and those who resisted it. "We had a couple people who started off extremely anti-AI, and they moved a little along the spectrum, but not enough, and so we ended up letting them go," the report quoted him as saying.

Ten companies, meanwhile, said they'd stepped up hiring because of AI, mainly to help roll it out or to boost IT support.

The pressure to keep up

The report also highlighted the anxiety workers feel about their roles in an AI-saturated workplace. One operations manager said she woke at 3 a.m. worried about her career prospects and turned to Claude, asking, "How do I make sure I set myself apart so that AI can't do everything that I do?"

While top-down approaches could rankle workers, letting workers experiment on their own brought a different set of problems, the report said. A tool that saved one person time didn't necessarily help others in a company. And apps that workers built still needed someone to review and maintain them.

At one law firm, a paralegal recalled the partners asking how he prompted AI after noticing that his demand letters stood out. He eventually agreed to share his approach with the firm, but his first instinct was to keep it to himself.

"That's my secret sauce," he told Anthropic.
